title: The Milky Way's Outer Disk Has Slowed Down, and Both Dark Matter and MOND May Have Predicted Wrong
dek: Gaia's rotation curve for the Milky Way's outer reaches looks Keplerian in its decline, while both dark matter halos and MOND expect it to stay flat — each side now needs tuned parameters or external field effects to survive.
why: 15 minutes lays out the latest data in the dark matter vs. MOND fight, with specific numbers and three possible explanations, for anyone who wants a quick read on where the field stands.
who: Physicists following dark matter, MOND or Milky Way dynamics, astronomy enthusiasts, and readers who want a fast take on the field's latest controversy.
skip: The methodological outlook after 13:30 can be skipped; the core conclusions are in the first 13 minutes.

points.h: A flat curve is where dark matter starts
points.body: What Vera Rubin and others observed is this: velocities in the outskirts of galaxies do not fall with radius, they stay roughly constant. By Kepler's laws, outer material is almost entirely enclosed, so velocity should decay like 1/√r; a constant velocity instead means the enclosed gravitational mass must keep rising with radius. Visible luminosity is fading while gravitational influence is not, and that mismatch is one of the clearest reasons dark matter became central to modern astrophysics. The standard explanation is a larger dark matter halo wrapped around the visible disk, emitting almost no light yet continuously contributing enclosed mass, which keeps the rotation curve flat.

points.h: We are measuring the pitch from inside the stands
points.body: Measuring the Milky Way has a built-in disadvantage: we are inside it. Keating's analogy is inferring the shape of an entire football pitch from inside the stands. Gaia provides precise measurements of stellar positions and motions, but it has no button labeled "true Milky Way rotation curve." To get a curve you must first choose a model, correct for asymmetric drift, assume equilibrium and symmetry, and then invert for circular velocity. The instrument supplies data; the pipeline tells us what those data points mean — revolutionary conclusions require looking at both chapters together.

points.h: Asymmetric drift gets deadlier the farther out you go
points.body: Stars do not travel on perfect circular orbits; they oscillate radially and vertically, which makes a stellar population's mean azimuthal velocity lower than the gravitational field's circular velocity — that difference is asymmetric drift. Recovering circular velocity requires modeling random motions. The problem is that the correction matters most precisely in the sparse outer regions, which is exactly where the enclosed mass is largest and the dispute is fiercest. The analysis infers a velocity decline of about 30 km/s between 19.5 and 26.5 kiloparsecs from the center, with a fitted outer slope of minus 0.47 plus or minus 0.15.

points.h: Turning a curve into mass rests entirely on geometric assumptions
points.body: If circular velocity really declines as 1/√r, then velocity squared declines as 1/r, and plugging that into the circular velocity equation gives a roughly constant enclosed spherical-equivalent mass — walking outward yet inferring almost no additional gravitational mass, which is awkward for a large, extended dark matter halo that should keep adding enclosed mass. But note the phrase "spherical equivalent": the Milky Way has a disk, gas, a bulge, a warp and a three-dimensional halo, and turning one curve into a mass requires a great deal of geometric insight.

points.h: 260 billion solar masses is below most independent estimates
points.body: The analysis gives a mean total mass estimate of about 2.6×10^11 solar masses, i.e. 260 billion solar masses, including stars, gas and dust, below many independent estimates that approach one trillion solar masses. That number comes from fitting the measured rotation curve and extrapolating the mass model beyond the region where stars directly constrain it. Gaia's rotation curve only constrains roughly 9 to 27 kiloparsecs, while the Milky Way's halo may extend to about 200 kiloparsecs, so most of the mass comes from the fitted model rather than direct tracers. Observation and extrapolation are not synonyms.

points.h: There is no radius in MOND's formula
points.body: MOND holds that below a certain characteristic acceleration, effective dynamics depart from Newtonian relations, and in the MOND regime acceleration is approximately the Newtonian acceleration times the square root of the MOND scale A0. In the low-acceleration limit, velocity to the fourth power equals Newton's constant times the baryonic mass times A0, and there is no radius in the equation — which is exactly why MOND naturally yields asymptotically flat rotation curves, and also its fragility. If the Milky Way's outer curve really is Keplerian in its decline, MOND likewise expected something flatter and did not find it. Dark matter and MOND reach flat curves through completely different physics, and a robust Keplerian decline would challenge both at once.

points.h: Defects lead to new laws, not to who won
points.body: Keating says defects lead to new laws; that is what he teaches his students. A Keplerian decline would not immediately falsify every version of MOND: MOND is nonlinear, external gravitational fields can influence a galaxy's internal dynamics and alter the Milky Way's outer behavior, and external field effects can produce a decline. So the defensible conclusion is not that Gaia killed MOND, but that a robust Keplerian curve would create tension with the isolated prediction, requiring external gravitational fields or other modifications to do a great deal of quantitative work. The test of a scientific claim is whether a theory can fit the measured curve with independent, justified parameters, not whether it can tell a nice story after the fact.

points.h: Distance errors, selection effects and the warp all muddy the picture
points.body: Distance errors change both a star's inferred position and its tangential velocity; asymmetric drift corrections depend on tracer density and velocity dispersion; selection effects change which stars enter the sample; the Milky Way's warp violates simple disk geometry; and the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy and the Large Magellanic Cloud also drive non-circular motions, acting like external gravitational mass. These tracers become sparse at large distances, and one must also question whether the stars are truly in equilibrium. In the Gaia analysis, neglected dynamical terms and the systematic error budget grow at the outermost radii. None of this proves the decline is fake, but it means that smooth curve may be masking a messy galaxy.

points.h: All three explanations are still alive
points.body: Keating offers three possibilities that remain viable: first, the decline is real but mild, and the Milky Way has a halo lighter or more concentrated than older models, so both dark matter and MOND can survive by tuning parameters; second, the decline is real but exaggerated, affected by systematics and non-equilibrium, which is the least glamorous answer and therefore one scientists must take seriously; third, the outer disk is perturbed enough that the reconstructed curve simply cannot be assumed to be equilibrium circular motion. One pattern, three possible physical stories, and the existing evidence cannot uniquely constrain or select any of them.

Different objects can be used to test it: dynamically colder Cepheids, stellar streams that probe farther out, and globular cluster satellites. Future Gaia data releases will improve astrometry, radio surveys will provide different tracers such as gas, and better theoretical models can explicitly incorporate the warp, the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy's effects and the Large Magellanic Cloud's effects. If the same decline is still recovered after combining different methods and different systematics, then you have to listen — it could go from 3 sigma to many sigma. But the Milky Way may be asking a trickier question: not whether dark matter lost or MOND won, but whether we are expecting the wrong curve.
